Drawers
drô'ērz
n. pl. (those who draw water; in Joshua, the servile class assigned to the Gibeonites)
From draw, Old English dragan, to pull. “Hewers of wood and drawers of water” became a proverbial phrase in English for the lowest servile labour.

Biblical Definition

The Gibeonites came to Joshua with mouldy bread and clouted shoes, pretending to be from a far country, and Israel “asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD” but made a league with them. When the deceit came out, the oath still bound: “Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation” (Jos 9:21). Joshua pronounced the curse and the appointment together: “there shall none of you be freed from being bondmen, and hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God” (Jos 9:23), and he “made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD…in the place which he should choose” (Jos 9:27). Two things follow, and both are large. First, an oath sworn in the LORD's name binds even when it was obtained by fraud, and Israel learned centuries later what it costs to break one: the famine in David's day was for Saul's slaughter of these same Gibeonites. Second, God took a people who lied their way into the covenant and set them to serve at His altar for ever. Nethinims stand in Ezra's returning lists. The curse became a place at the house of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a drawer as one who draws, particularly one who draws liquor or water; and, in Scripture, a servile labourer.

expand to see more

DRAWER, n. One who draws or pulls; one who takes water from a well.

2. He that draws liquor for guests; a waiter in a tavern.

Hewers of wood and drawers of water. Josh. ix.

Key Scripture

Jos 9:21 — "And the princes said unto them, Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation; as the princes had promised them."

Jos 9:27 — "And Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose."

Psa 15:4 — "In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."

Modern Corruption

An oath is now treated as a statement of present intention, revocable when circumstances change, and the Gibeonite episode is exactly the case Scripture uses to teach the opposite.

expand to see more

Joshua 9 is the hardest possible test case for the binding force of a vow, and Scripture decides it against Israel's convenience. The league was obtained by lying. Israel was under standing orders to make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land. The princes had failed in the one duty that would have exposed the fraud — they asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. Every ground a modern conscience would use to void the agreement was present, and the princes still said, We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them. Psalm 15 makes that very disposition a mark of the man who shall abide in God's tabernacle: he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. And 2 Samuel 21 shows the cost of the opposite: three years of famine in David's reign because Saul, centuries later, slew the Gibeonites in his zeal, breaking an oath he had not made. Modern practice treats promises — marital, contractual, congregational — as commitments held for as long as they serve the parties. Ecclesiastes 5:5 gives the older wisdom: better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay. The Gibeonites, meanwhile, are the standing proof that God can put a deceiver to work at His altar and keep him there.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sha'ab (H7579), to draw water; chatab (H2404), to cut or hew wood; nathiyn (H5411), the Nethinims, the given ones who served the temple.

expand to see more

Hebrew sha'ab (H7579) — to draw water from a well; the daily labour of the women at evening and of the Gibeonites for ever; Genesis 24:11, Joshua 9:21.

Hebrew chatab (H2404) — to hew or gather wood; the paired half of the proverbial phrase; Joshua 9:21, Deuteronomy 29:11.

Hebrew nathiyn (H5411) — the Nethinims, the given ones, temple servants listed among the returning exiles; Ezra 2:43, Nehemiah 7:46.

Usage

"“Hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation” — the sentence on the Gibeonite deceit."

"“For the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD” — the servitude assigned to the house of God."

"“He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” — the psalm that vindicates Israel's refusal to break the oath."
